beyond_this_part.why: No note in this part changes the identity of any person, the meaning of a rope term established earlier, or the reading of an earlier passage; the terms standardised here — high-hands/low-hands and the ganjigarame cross-lattice bind — are fixed within this part's own catalogue at p25.

declined.reason: Declined. 米利堅 and 和蘭陀 are place-names the narrator treats as known; rendering them as America and Holland keeps the period flavour through the surrounding talk of the national ban, Yoshida Shōin and Fujita's prophecy, while adding 'Meriken, to America, or to Oranda, to Holland' is expansion and clarification that doubles every name in O-Tetsu's speech and slows her cajoling. The reading asks for period flavour, not for transliterated names with glosses in the line.

Declined the suggested wording, though the fragment is noted. The Japanese list itself runs as an inventory closed by 鉄扇を手に持つばかり, and the English inventory keeps that staccato dressing-up rhythm, which the reading protects against rationalisation; 'He wore' smooths it into ordinary narration. The suggested 'light-lined kimono' for 初袷 is also not settled, and I will not put an unsettled garment term into the text.

Declined the suggested wording. As with p67, the Japanese gives the monk's get-up as a performed inventory — coat, sash, tucked-up hem, headband — before any verb of action, and the English fragment preserves that music-hall entrance; supplying 'He wore' tidies it. 'Workman's coat' for 納所着 also drops the temple-servant specificity the passage needs for a fallen monk.

Declined. 'What ... looked like blood spraying ... was the red dragonflies' treats what was seen as one impression, which is how the Japanese stages it: first the false sight, then the correction. Changing 'was' to 'were' makes the reader agree the verb with dragonflies before the mis-seeing has registered. 'Crepe' for 'chirimen' is taken up in R18 below.

Declined. 白毫刻する如く is a precise, strange image — the kozuka standing in the monk's brow as if carving the Buddha's white curl — and the translator's note already gives the reader the byakugō. 'Like a Buddha's brow-mark' explains the image instead of letting it strike, which is clarification; the reading says to keep the strangeness and let the margin carry what the sentence cannot.

Declined. 意味深く覚えられる is the narrator pausing to savour the point, and 'deeply pointed' keeps both the savouring and the point; 'deeply telling' and 'reuse of worn-out things' flatten 廃物利用, whose slight bureaucratic flatness is part of the joke that capture-ropes become ferry-ropes. This is the digressive voice the reading forbids us to sleek away.

Declined. 円め込められて is rolled up, rounded into the palm, and 'rolled in the palm of her hand ... like a plaything' keeps the physical comedy of a 500-koku swordsman being handled like a toy, which is the humiliation the crux turns on. 'Held in the palm of her hand' is the smoother English idiom and loses exactly the rolling the Japanese insists on.

Declined the suggested form. The complaint is about register, but the suggested 'disagreeing with his stomach' merely repeats 'stomach' after 'stomach pain' and is no less modern; the present wording keeps the suspicion at p21 as suspicion, which is what that passage must not lose, and does not turn 中って into poisoning.

Declined the suggested form. 'Those cut off from one' renders 隔絶している人, people cut off by distance and by the absence of telegraph, telephone and post; the suggested 'those far away' weakens the severance that the whole dream-essay is built on, and 'the mind is left to run on by itself' loses 想像を走らせる, the imagination set running. The essay's slightly discursive gait is deliberate and is kept.

Declined. 唐縮緬 appears again at p142 as 'chirimen', and the rope-and-fabric vocabulary of this text must stay in one recognisable set rather than be varied for elegance; 'imported-crepe' at p139 and 'crepe' later would break that consistency. The faded red waistcloth against the mud is a lingering image the reading protects, and an unexplained fabric word there is a matter for the margin, not for paraphrase in the line.

Declined, and recorded as a disagreement below. 其前の妻女 is 'his previous wife'; in the flat coda the point is sequence — Kotora first, then the Meiji detective's later life — and 'former wife' in this flat register does not import a divorce narrative strongly enough to override the Japanese, which states only that she died early in Meiji.

disagreements.choice: F11's wording was taken: 'you might well have suspected blood ran and a pulse beat'.
disagreements.faithful_side: F11: 怪しまれる is to suspect, not to doubt, so the sentence must say the weeds seemed to have blood and a pulse (F11 on p156).
disagreements.readable_side: R12 agreed the sense was inverted but proposed 'you might have thought even the water-weeds had blood running and pulses beating in them', which softens 怪しまれる into a general thought.

disagreements.choice: Both notes were taken together: 'out of spite' for the incomplete 'in spite', 'began' for 'opened her mouth', and 'vexation' for 'regret'.
disagreements.faithful_side: F8: 口惜しい is vexation or mortification, not the remorse 'regret' implies, and O-Tetsu feels no remorse.
disagreements.readable_side: R4: 'in spite' lacks an object in English and 'opened her mouth' is dictionary-literal for beginning to speak.

disagreements.choice: R1's clean sentence was taken: 'O-Tetsu vindictively kicked her as she lay and even spat on her.'
disagreements.faithful_side: F14 proposed 'with vindictive tenacity', keeping 執念深く as tenacity as well as spite.
disagreements.readable_side: R1 proposed the same sentence without 'tenacity', on the ground that the stray non-English characters make the line unreadable.

disagreements.choice: The text stands as 'former wife'; R19 is declined for the reason given above. The reading settles this — the coda must stay flat and must not be made to explain the marriage — so it does not go up.
disagreements.faithful_side: No faithful note on p224; the Japanese 其前の妻女 says no more than 'his wife before', and the translator kept the circles and the shrug exactly.
disagreements.readable_side: R19: 'former wife' implies divorce in English and misleads the coda, where Kotora is his dead first wife.

disagreements.choice: No change. The catalogue at p25 is the standard, and both later echoes — 高手小手 at p42 and the ganjigarame at p164 — were brought back to its exact terms, because the reading makes that echo the engine of the underwater fight rather than ornament.
disagreements.faithful_side: F7 and F13: the catalogue's set terms must recur unchanged — low hands, not small-hands (p42), and the ganjigarame cross-lattice bind, not hold (p164).
disagreements.readable_side: No readable note defended the variation; the readable notes on these paragraphs concerned other matters.

disagreements.choice: The text stands ('Who the shit would let you have it'), and this goes up to the editor, because the reading requires the monk's music-hall vulgarity to stay at the original's level and the choice of English obscenity is a house-level register call that being wrong on would matter for every later line of his abuse.
disagreements.faithful_side: No faithful note on the wording; 狗鼠 is a term of abuse ('dog-rat') hurled at the couple, and a literal transfer keeps the insult aimed at them.
disagreements.readable_side: R17: 'Who the shit' is not speakable English abuse and sounds like a machine swap; it proposes 'Like hell I'd let you have it', which is idiomatic but redirects the insult from the couple to the speaker's refusal.

data.say: Desk done. Most notes were a reader catching something real and were taken in the smallest form: the double-sandal idiom at p7, 'taking men prisoner' at p9, rumour 'to be heard' at p10, the missing main verb at p15, single-heir transmission at p28, 'flatter him as they might' at p35, 'achieved his aim' at p4, the dangling night-boat opener at p13, the shoulder image at p31, 'anticipated his every want' at p33, the standardised high-hands/low-hands at p42 with 'out of spite ... full of vexation', 'as plain as if beside us' at p127, the reversed suspect/doubt at p156, the dart expansion cut at p160, the ganjigarame cross-lattice bind restored at p164, the corrupted characters removed at p214, the self-made rust idiom at p191, and the hair-pulled reluctance marked as a feeling at p71. Declined, with reasons the reader can follow: F9 (America/Holland kept; transliteration plus gloss would be expansion in O-Tetsu's speech), R7 and R8 (the verbless costume inventories keep the Japanese listing rhythm, and the suggested garment terms are unsettled), R9 (the was/were change breaks the staged mis-seeing), R10 (the Buddha's white curl stays literal; explanation belongs in the margin), R11 ('deeply pointed' keeps the narrator savouring 廃物利用), R14 ('rolled in the palm' keeps 円め込められて and the plaything comedy), R15 (the suggested wording is no less modern and repeats 'stomach'), R16 ('cut off' keeps 隔絶, the severance the dream-essay turns on), R18 (chirimen must stay one consistent term across p139 and p142), and R19 ('former wife' kept for 其前の妻女 in the flat coda). Two reader pairs overlapped rather than disagreed and were taken together: F8/R4 at p42 and F14/R1 at p214; at p156 F11 and R12 agreed on the sense and F11's 'suspected' was taken. One place goes up to the editor: the monk's abuse at p126, where the readable reader's 'Like hell I'd let you have it' is speakable but redirects the insult, and the literal 'Who the shit' is not speakable English — the reading fixes the level of vulgarity but not the English form. Nothing in this part requires an earlier part to be taken back. House log: the desk held the rope catalogue's terms as the standard for every later echo, took the idiom and grammar notes in their smallest form, and declined the notes that would have glossed, smoothed or explained what the text leaves strange.
